articles.title: Huracán Simón de categoría 4 EN VIVO | nueva trayectoria, cuándo y dónde tocará tierra en México
articles.summary: El lento desplazamiento del huracán Simón frente a Jalisco amenaza con prolongar los efectos más severos en la costa de México, con vientos de hasta 230 km/h, olas de nueve metros y lluvias extraordinarias
articles.body_text: Los últimos pronósticos del domingo redujeron las posibilidades de que el huracán Simón toque tierra en México, sin que disminuyan los riesgos de fuertes lluvias y vientos severos. El ciclón avanza a un ritmo peligrosamente lento y paralelo a la costa del Pacífico en una categoría 4 de 5 en la escala Saffir Simpson. Los efectos suelen golpear más a medida que pasa más tiempo en un mismo lugar. Pero “parece estar sintiendo los efectos del terreno alto” de la cadena montañosa que atraviesa esta región, indicó la agencia de huracanes de Estados Unidos (NHC) en su boletín más reciente. El NHC observó que es “cada vez más probable que Simón evite tocar tierra directamente a corto plazo”. El gobierno mexicano prevé “que se debilite paulatinamente durante las próximas horas”, según su último reporte. Un equipo de la AFP fue a Puerto Vallarta, una joya turística que será golpeada por los efectos del huracán. Las autoridades piden a los paseantes alejarse del malecón. Las olas rompían con fuerza sobre este paseo y el agua rebasaba una estatua de un caballito de mar de unos dos metros. “Ven la ola y parece que les dicen arrímense (acérquense)”, reprochó una policía sobre un grupo de turistas que se acerca a tomar fotos e ignora la indicación de alejarse de la orilla. “Vemos a varias personas que les cuesta un poco acatar indicaciones y se ponen en riesgo”, indicó la oficial Claudia Matías. Los negocios protegieron ventanas y puertas con tablones, y en algunos pintaron en aerosol mensajes como “Simón dice: ‘todo va a estar bien’”, en referencia al popular juego en el que los niños siguen instrucciones, o “Simón, sé breve, pacífico” junto al dibujo de un tiburón y caras felices. Manuel Jaime, habitante de Vallarta de 37 años, caminaba en la acera de enfrente, llena de negocios tapiados. Salió a pasear con su familia para relajarse. “En esta ocasión parece ser que va a estar muy tranquilo el puerto, esperemos que sí”, dijo. Pero la intensidad de la lluvia y la marea incrementa hacia la tarde. Vicente García, un turista de 48 años, proveniente de California, coincide. “Esperábamos una tormenta más grande ayer, así que permanecimos adentro, pero me alegra que no fuera así”, indicó. “Ya nos vamos mañana”. Por la mañana el gobierno mexicano estimó que hacia las 18H00 locales del domingo el centro del ciclón llegaría a unos 15 km de las costas del estado de Jalisco. Aunque no toque tierra “todas las bandas nubosas del ciclón o la parte intensa del ciclón de todos modos va a estar afectando” poblados a la orilla del mar, explicó a la AFP el director del servicio meteorológico de México, Fabián Vázquez. “Vamos a tener efectos muy severos sobre todo de viento en la costa” con olas de hasta nueve metros y lluvias extraordinarias, añadió. El sábado, la Marina de México evacuó por barco a un centenar de personas de poblados costeros amenazados por Simón. En Puerto Vallarta, decenas de habitantes comenzaron a llegar a los refugios provenientes de colonias en riesgo por inundaciones. “A lo mejor si llega el huracán, va a levantar la casa y por eso mejor decidimos venir a un refugio”, dice José de Jesús Santillán, albañil de 55 años, sentado en un camastro. En otro albergue permanece Raquel García, de 58 años. Vive en una zona de riesgo por inundaciones. Pero no le preocupan demasiado las pérdidas materiales. “Con el tiempo, lo vamos a recuperar (...) yo prefiero mi vida y la de mi esposo que las cosas”.

articles.title: Veritas expands its anti-counterfeit chip to jewelry, trophies, and fragrance bottles | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Counterfeits of luxury goods are a major problem for fashion houses. Counterfeiters are getting better at replicating brands' marks and passing off dupes,
articles.body_text: Counterfeits of luxury goods are a major problem for fashion houses. Counterfeiters are getting better at replicating brands’ marks and passing off dupes, known as “ superfakes ,” as genuine items. A startup called Veritas wants to tackle the problem with its own chip that verifies goods. Veritas was founded by Luci Holland, a former Tesla technical product manager who also has a background in design and art. Its chip is built to be easily inserted into products without damaging them. Brands can use it to verify whether a product is the real deal, and customers can show a certificate of ownership through the company’s app. Holland said other approaches are easier to defeat, because a digital record can be reproduced through a copied QR code or static NFC link. “Our approach combines secure, authenticated chip responses with integration into the product itself. Our chip generates a secure response with each tap and includes a tamper-detection wire. We make the connection between the object and its digital identity part of the proof,” Holland said. The Veritas founder told TechCrunch over email that the company has just introduced the second version of its chip, which works on metal surfaces and can be scanned through glass. “The next-generation chip is ready for production and supports a broader range of applications, including jewelry, trophies, hard-surface products, and glass objects such as fragrance bottles,” Holland said. “Alongside our garment integrations, this gives brands more ways to incorporate authentication directly into their products.” This week, the startup announced a partnership with ATHLOS, a women’s track-and-field competition founded by Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian, who is also an investor in Veritas. As part of the partnership, all 18 championship crowns will include Veritas’ chips so they can be verified. The company also embedded a chip into a pair of LeBron James’ first Nike shoes, reimagined by artist Adam Port. Tapping a phone to the shoe brings up its history and story. The company has so far raised $1.75 million in pre-seed funding led by Ohanian’s venture firm Seven Seven Six, with participation from DoorDash co-founder Stanley Tang; Gloria Zhu, co-founder of skincare brand Reys; and former TechCrunch editor Josh Constine. Since its February fundraise, the company has shipped an iOS app for consumers and a brand portal that lets companies manage product records and build owner experiences. Through the app and the portal, brands can offer experiences such as clubs, event check-ins, and segmented early access to product drops. Veritas competed in this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt Startup Battlefield, which ran Tuesday through Thursday. A winner was announced Thursday afternoon . articles.body_text: Meta has launched what it calls the “most capable” open-weight model in the United States. Dubbed Muse Spark Open, the model also has the distinction of having been designed to work with Macs. The new model, which leverages 816 billion parameters and a 1 million token context window, claims to offer superior performance to other popular open-weight models, according to evaluation results released by Meta on Thursday. Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and built for complex coding tasks and agentic labor. It has also been designed to run locally on Apple’s computers. However, you will still need a lot of power to run the model locally, with a requirement of at least 1 terabyte of RAM, per Engadget . The model will run best via the Mac Studio that comes equipped with the M5 Ultra chip. Still, if you can muster the memory, Muse Spark Open may prove a significant work horse for coding and other desktop tasks. Meta says that it paired the model with Muse Code, its AI coding terminal, and deployed it to various agentic workflows, including coding fixes for a Mastodon client that included “bug fixes, new features, [and] full build.” The company says it also deployed it in the service of running DaVinci Resolve, the high-end video editing software, revealing that the model was capable of reviewing and cropping footage. Open-weight models provide a number of distinct industry advantages that aren’t afforded by closed and proprietary models. Open-weight models can be significantly more cost-efficient and can also offer transparency and flexibility that closed source models don’t allow. articles.title: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay sees a future where AI devices replace the need to use apps | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt, Amazon devices chief Panos Panay described a future where ambient AI devices work in the background, anticipating users' needs instead of waiting for commands.
articles.body_text: Amazon is placing its bets on ambient computing, not apps, as the future of personal AI. Alongside the launch of the company’s new AI wearables from Bee , Panos Panay, who serves as Amazon’s SVP of Devices, Alexa & Leo, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday to talk more in depth about where he sees personal computing headed. “A lot of times, what you’re doing right now — what we all do right now — is we have to remember what we’re asking our tool to do for us,” Panay began, explaining that this is how we engage with our modern smartphones. “It’s like point, shoot, return,” Panay continued. “I think where we’re headed is a world [that] starts with ambient devices.” By “ambient devices,” he means those that work quietly in the background, using sensors and AI to help you figure out what needs to be done, instead of the other way around, where you’re telling the device what you need to do. “As it works in the background, you’re able to stay more present. You’re able to get more done. You’re about to spend more time with people … you’re not afraid if you miss something. It’s incredibly powerful,” Panay said. Amazon’s biggest entry into this space is the set of new Bee devices it introduced on Thursday, which include a band you can wear on your wrist or detach to wear as a pendant, as well as a new credit-card-sized device that attaches magnetically to the back of your smartphone. The executive, who came to Amazon after 19 years at Microsoft where he oversaw the development of Surface devices, has spent a lot of his life thinking about how personal computing will evolve. With Bee — and ambient computing more generally — Panay also envisioned a future where the idea of interacting with apps becomes less important, as more tasks are handled via AI. “Do I think we have a future where there’s a bit of a balance — a whole generation that doesn’t say ‘give me the app’ for that, but says it should just understand what I need? Yeah, I do. I think that transformation is coming. I think that is the next generation,” he said. That doesn’t necessarily mean the smartphone itself won’t continue to be an important personal computing device (as much as Amazon would like it to be an Alexa tablet or Echo smart speaker), Panay pointed out. Rather, he believes a new crop of devices will emerge that use sensors to understand users better, and to bring intelligence to the world around you. “I’m not a proponent that says one form factor is going to replace another. I don’t think that’s the case,” he clarified. “I think there’s an intelligence layer that connects it all … and it has to be useful.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . articles.title: Anthropic is letting METR researchers look under the hood with employee-level access | TechCrunch
articles.summary: METR will publish its own assessments of Anthropic’s risks, incidents, and practices, and the frontier AI model maker has given up the right to block them.
articles.body_text: Anthropic is giving employee-level access to six researchers from METR , a nonprofit that tests frontier AI models, to independently assess Anthropic’s models, safety practices, and risk management, the company said in a blog post on Thursday. The arrangement comes at a time where incidents of AI agents acting outside their instructions have been disclosed every week or two since late August. The incidents have sharpened calls for independent checks on AI companies. “We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making,” Anthropic said in the blog post. “We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.” Under the new arrangement, the METR team has Anthropic-issued company laptops, office space, and access to internal tools roughly on par with what Anthropic’s own risk assessment teams use. “Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk” the company said. Anthropic compared the arrangement to banking, similar to how regulators place resident examiners inside the largest banks. METR will publish its own assessments of Anthropic’s risks, incidents, and practices, and the company has given up the right to block them. “Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into narrow, pre-defined categories,” the company said, such as customer data, anything attorney-client privileged, or relating to information about its model architectures. “METR is free to characterize our redactions publicly, and say whether it believes the redactions were justified, as long as it does so without revealing the redacted information” Anthropic added. METR is the only evaluator so far at the top of a three-tier system Anthropic is building. Evaluators in the bottom tier, like biosecurity nonprofit SecureBio, run narrow reviews and require Anthropic’s approval to publish. The middle tier gets more information and can publish without approval, while the top tier adds METR’s employee-level access. Thursday’s announcement makes good on a promise Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei made in a September essay , where he proposed embedding outside evaluators inside AI labs as a first step toward slowing the technology’s development. OpenAI quickly pledged the same , and both companies, along with Google, Meta, Nvidia, and xAI, have since signed a White House accord committing to independent review. articles.title: Bluesky expands its AI-powered Attie app to let anyone build websites, games, and more | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Bluesky is bringing “social vibe coding” to its experimental Attie platform, allowing users to create interactive experiences like games, quizzes, and websites that can tap into the social network's audience.
articles.body_text: Open social network Bluesky is once again expanding beyond its flagship app. At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 on Thursday, the company announced the launch of a new tool that allows creators to make websites, quizzes, games, polls, and other interactive experiences. The tool is an expansion of Attie, Bluesky’s more experimental platform , which initially offered AI-powered technology for building custom social feeds. With its new creation capabilities, the idea is to allow everyday users to create the kind of experiences that previously only software developers could build. These user-created games, sites, and other experiences will also live on the same AT Protocol (ATProto) that powers Bluesky and other decentralized social apps that make up the decentralized social web known as the Atmosphere. Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider shared the news of Attie’s new capabilities during an interview at Disrupt, saying, “We’re adding a feature to our Attie product that allows you to build sites and social experiences again for a group of people. So think of it as … social vibe coding or vibe coding for your community.” The exec, a former CEO of Automattic and a partner at True Ventures, had previously been leading the company on an interim basis after former CEO Jay Graber stepped down in March to become Bluesky’s chief innovation officer. Now he’s taking charge of the company as it enters the AI era. Attie offers Bluesky a playground where it can try out AI-powered ideas like this. “Vibe coding today is kind of a single-user, solo experience,” Schneider explained. “And what I want to be able to do is build together or build for a group of people, and that’s what this product does.” When creators build with Attie, they’re connected to their ATProto identity. Plus, Attie will suggest things users might want to make based on their public Bluesky profiles. To build with Attie, users can bring their own AI model or use open-weight options, and the resulting sites and games can then tap into Bluesky’s wider audience, noted Bluesky COO Rose Wang. “Everybody is building … But the big question is: Who’s using the thing you’re building, because we haven’t solved that problem with distribution,” she said. “What makes Attie so interesting is that it comes with the Bluesky distribution, so it doesn’t stand alone.” That network today has 47 million registered users , though it’s seen a decline in engagement , as some users who tested it out later returned to X. Beyond being a testing ground for new ideas, Attie ties into Bluesky’s larger plans to reinvigorate activity on its network by focusing on both developers and communities in the months ahead. Those areas will also be supercharged by the protocol’s forthcoming support for private data, which Schneider said has been the biggest request from developers. Private data is now in alpha testing, with plans for a rollout by the end of the year, he said.

articles.title: Ramp reaches $60B valuation as it pushes deeper into AI | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The funding comes as Ramp's annualized revenue crosses $2B, and its customer count reaches 85,000.
articles.body_text: Expense management company Ramp said on Thursday that it had raised $1.85 billion in a new funding round that values it at $60 billion, just four months after raising $750 million at a $44 billion valuation . The financing was co-led by Dragoneer Investment Group, Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Sands Capital, and Avenir Growth. Ramp said its annualized revenue has crossed $2 billion, up from a reported $1.5 billion in June, and that its revenue growth is 25% faster than it was around this time last year. The company claims it now facilitates annualized purchase volume of over $275 billion, up 175% from a year earlier. It also says it has 85,000 customers, up from 70,000 in June, including Visa, Uber, Shopify, Robinhood, Anduril, Notion, Cursor, and Figma. The funding comes as Ramp has been expanding beyond expense management into payments, fraud detection, procurement, vendor management, and, of late, even accounting. The startup has also built an AI story around itself, embedding AI agents into its procurement, expense management, accounting, budgeting, and other products. It also launched a corporate credit card specifically designed for AI agents to use, and in August entered the model routing business to tap the booming AI inference market and give existing clients a model routing service that fits neatly with its current products, including AI token usage monitoring and token spend management. Earlier this month, Ramp launched Glass , a workspace that collects and remembers the AI automations, prompts, and skills that an organization’s employees build so others can take advantage of the company’s collective knowledge and skills. “In just a few years, Ramp has become a much broader financial operations platform, with AI deeply embedded in how the company builds and operates. We believe Ramp is well on its way to becoming one of the defining companies of this era,” Christian Jensen, partner at Dragoneer, said in a statement. Other investors in the round include Capital International, Fidelity Management & Research Company, T. Rowe Price, D1 Capital Partners, Greenoaks, ICONIQ, GIC, 8VC, 1789 Capital, Alpha Wave Global, Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan, Coatue, D.E. Shaw, Definition Capital, FirstMark, General Catalyst, Generation Investment Management, Glade Brook Capital Partners, Khosla Ventures, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Pinegrove Opportunity Partners, Soma Capital, and Stripes. The company has now raised about $5 billion in funding. As Ramp has widened its product lineup, it has increasingly run into Rippling, the HR and payroll software company that has pushed into corporate cards, expense management, and bill payments. The overlap puts the two companies in direct competition for the same finance-team budgets. Early investor Keith Rabois, who has backed Ramp through two firms, Founders Fund and Khosla Ventures, both of which participated in this round, spoke to TechCrunch last month about Ramp’s strategy and his own big ambitions for the company. “Ramp is not worried about Rippling,” Rabois said. “We’re going to compete with Anthropic,” he continued. “That’s the goal. I want to be larger and more successful and more important than Anthropic. Ramp is going to be the primary way people manage their token spend, how they optimize it, how they measure ROI, and that will lead us to collide probably with Anthropic in many ways.”

articles.title: Ron DeSantis signs bill requiring parental consent for kids under 16 to hold social media accounts
articles.summary: Republican Governor Ron DeSantis vetoed an earlier bill in Florida that would have restricted social media accounts for kids under 16, but HB 3 allows for more parental consent.
articles.body_text: Florida Governor Ron DeSantis (R) just signed into law HB 3, a bill that will give parents of teens under 16 more control over their kids’ access to social media and require age verification for many websites. The bill requires social media platforms to prevent kids under 14 from creating accounts, and delete existing ones. It also requires parent or guardian consent for 14- and 15-year-olds to create or maintain social media accounts and mandates that platforms delete social media accounts and personal information for this age group at the teen’s or parent’s request. Companies that fail to promptly delete accounts belonging to 14- and 15-year-olds can be sued on behalf of those kids and may owe them up to $10,000 in damages each. A “knowing or reckless” violation could also be considered an unfair or deceptive trade practice, subject to up to $50,000 in civil penalties per violation. The bill also requires many commercial apps and websites to verify their users’ ages — something that introduces a host of privacy concerns. But it does require websites to give users the option of “anonymous age verification,” which is defined as verification by a third party that cannot retain identifying information after the task is complete. The requirement kicks in when a commercial site contains a “substantial portion of material harmful to minors,” defined as more than a third of content on the site, which would clearly target porn sites in particular. Such sites must ensure users are 18 or older — though news sites are exempt from the requirement. Violations are also subject to an up to $50,000 civil penalty each. Tech industry groups have already come out against the legislation. NetChoice — an association representing major social media platforms that’s already embroiled in a Supreme Court battle with the state over a separate social media law — said before HB 3 was signed that it “in effect will impose an ‘I.D. for the Internet’ on any Floridian who wants to use an online service—regardless of their age.” The governor vetoed an earlier social media bill that would have banned social media accounts for kids under 16. Unlike the newly signed legislation, the one DeSantis vetoed wouldn’t have given parents the option to okay their 14- and 15-year-olds’ accounts. “Protecting children from harms associated with social media is important, as is supporting parents’ rights and maintaining the ability of adults to engage in anonymous speech,” DeSantis tweeted on the day he vetoed the earlier bill. DeSantis has staked much of his political capital on championing parents’ rights over the sort of information kids have access to. He signed the Parental Rights in Education Act in 2022, which opponents call the “Don’t Say Gay” law, that bars schools from discussing sexual orientation or gender identity for some grades. Another bill DeSantis approved strengthened parents’ ability to challenge books in school libraries and reading lists. Florida’s action follows other states’ moves to limit teen social media access or require greater parental insight into their kids’ online activities. Last year, for example, Utah’s governor signed into law two bills that require kids under 18 to get parental consent to use social media and would give parents access to kids’ posts and messages online. Soon after, Arkansas’ governor approved a bill similarly requiring parental consent for minors in the state to open social media accounts. DeSantis hasn’t shied away from regulating social media companies in the past. In 2021, he signed into law SB 7072, which requires social media companies to enforce content moderation in a “consistent” manner and prevent them from deplatforming political candidates or so-called journalistic enterprises. The Supreme Court is currently considering whether the law violates the First Amendment by forcing private companies to carry speech even when they don’t want to. Florida House Speaker Paul Renner (R) said at a press conference for the bill signing Monday that they took pains to avoid First Amendment issues with HB 3. “You will not find a line in this bill that addresses good speech or bad speech because that would violate the First Amendment,” Renner said. “We’ve not addressed that at all. What we have addressed is the addictive features that are at the heart of why children stay on these platforms for hours and hours on end.” Renner compared the addictive features of social media to drinking alcohol, and said kids are not yet equipped to moderate themselves. “Unlike an adult who can make an adult decision say I drank too much last night, I need to drink less or stop drinking altogether, a child in their brain development doesn’t have the ability to know that they’re being sucked in to these addictive technologies, and to see the harm, and step away from it. And because of that, we have to step in for them.” Legislation targeting social media platforms for how they protect young users has become increasingly popular over the past few years. A leading proposal in the US Senate, the Kids Online Safety Act, recently passed the threshold of support needed to clear that chamber, once scheduled for a vote. And another proposal in the Senate, the Protecting Kids on Social Media Act, would require parental consent for kids under 18 to use social media. The Florida legislation is set to take effect on January 1st next year.

The moral bankruptcy of Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz
articles.summary: Two of the most famous investors in Silicon Valley endorsed Donald Trump. This is less about tech generally than their investment portfolio, specifically.
articles.body_text: Last week, the founders of venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz declared their allegiance to Donald Trump in their customary fashion: talking about money on a podcast. “Sorry, Mom,” Ben Horowitz says in an episode of The Ben & Marc Show. “I know you’re going to be mad at me for this. But, like, we have to do it.” Marc Andreessen and Horowitz insist they voted for Democrats until now. They are friends with liberals. They claim to be nervous about the social blowback they will receive for this, especially because of the historically progressive nature of the tech industry and the Bay Area. But given the general movement among their class toward Trump, I think those claims about being nervous are overblown, if not performative. There is, for instance, Elon Musk’s pro-Trump super PAC, which has support from Sequoia Capital’s Shaun Maguire and 8VC’s Joe Lonsdale, among other notables. (The Wall Street Journal reported Musk is planning to donate $45 million a month, which Musk has denied.) There’s the $160 million the crypto movement has put forward in support of crypto-friendly candidates. We can’t forget their VC pal David Sacks speaking at the Republican National Convention. And last but not least, there’s Trump’s running mate choice of JD Vance, a former venture capitalist whose firm’s investors included Peter Thiel, Eric Schmidt, and Andreessen himself. This isn’t a movement. It’s a clique. The podcast itself is an extraordinary performance. At one point, Andreessen concedes that their major problems with President Joe Biden — the ones that led them to support Trump — are what most voters would consider “subsidiary” issues. “It doesn’t have anything to do with the big issues that people care about,” he says. If we take this podcast at face value, we are to believe that these subsidiary issues are the only reason they’ve chosen to endorse and donate to Trump. These subsidiary issues take precedence for Andreessen and Horowitz over, say, mass deportations and Project 2025’s attempt to end no-fault divorce. We are looking at a simple trade against personal liberty — abortion, the rights of gay and trans people, and possibly democracy itself — in favor of crypto, AI, and a tax policy they like better. For Horowitz, “probably the most emotional topic” is crypto — a16z started a $4.5 billion crypto fund in 2022, and the pair believe that the Biden administration has been deeply unfair to crypto. In Horowitz’s view, the Biden administration “basically subverted the rule of law to attack the crypto industry.” Certainly much of the crypto industry prefers Trump. But it seems obvious that there has been a lot of intra-agency squabbling as Congress dithered on passing any laws. To place the blame squarely on Biden is bizarre, particularly when we have Trump’s chaotic previous term as guidance. Sure, Trump is no longer saying Bitcoin is “a scam against the dollar,” as he did in 2021; he is scheduled to speak at the Bitcoin conference this year. But his record in office is not exactly pro-crypto. During the Trump administration, financial regulator FinCEN initially asked the public to provide comments on a crypto rule change over a 15-day period that included Christmas Eve, Christmas Day, New Year’s Eve, and New Year’s Day, which effectively shortened the comment window by four working days. There is also the Ripple Labs enforcement case, in which the SEC is seeking a $1.95 billion fine; it, too, dates to the Trump administration. The pair’s complaints about Gary Gensler, the current head of the Securities and Exchange Commission, are striking. They are particularly annoyed that he won’t pay attention to them. “We’re the largest crypto investors or largest blockchain investors in the world, and we’ve requested meetings with him at least a half a dozen times,” Horowitz says. Gensler has not met with them. Neither, they say, has Senator Elizabeth Warren or Biden himself. In fact, Andreessen makes it clear that he expects presidential attention, something he’s been getting since he was 23. Given the number of times Andreessen and Horowitz make references to various meetings with various politicians, it’s easy to get the impression that they are mostly insulted that they are being treated like ordinary constituents. From crypto, we move to AI, which Andreessen and Horowitz don’t think is being regulated correctly either. According to Horowitz, AI is as powerful as, or more powerful than, the internet and the global computer industry from the 1950s on. “This may be the biggest technological boom of all time,” Andreessen says. Andreessen says in his newsletter-cum-manifesto, “The Little Tech Agenda,” that he is worried that AI will face similar scrutiny to crypto. The FTC has issued guidance to the AI industry that indicated it will pursue companies that exaggerate what their AI can do, say they are using AI when they are not, and recklessly put products on the market without properly analyzing the risks. Meanwhile, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has told lenders that they must supply a reason for a credit denial that’s better than just “computer says no” when using AI models. These regulations have little to do with technology and a lot to do with old-fashioned lying. In the podcast, Andreessen and Horowitz single out Biden’s executive order about artificial intelligence. The order requires companies to disclose the presence of very large models, as well as to provide the government information about what the plans are for the model, what cybersecurity measures are taken to protect those models, and the results of red-team testing for sensitive subjects, among other things. This is in keeping with Horowitz’s assertion about the seriousness of the technology. So what’s the problem? The two focus on computing power. The disclosure requirements apply to “any model that was trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 1026 integer or floating-point operations, or using primarily biological sequence data and using a quantity of computing power greater than 1023 integer or floating-point operations.” Andreessen and Horowitz think specifying such a limit is ridiculous. Little tech “will be snuffed out by this kind of regulation,” Horowitz says. It is perhaps worth noting that nothing above the size specified in the executive order — the size Andreessen and Horowitz object to — even exists yet, according to Arati Prabhakar, Biden’s top tech advisor. The fundamental complaint here is that these two believe that the Biden administration’s approach to AI “enshrine[s] the two or three companies that they believe are the only companies that matter as sort of permanent monopolies,” Andreessen says. “And they’re going to just basically destroy the startup ecosystem underneath that.” Andreessen Horowitz is, of course, invested in that ecosystem, having earmarked $2.25 billion for AI applications and infrastructure. The anti-monopoly rhetoric is in keeping with a16z’s latest marketing push. According to Andreessen’s newsletter, startups are threatened by the government, which is “now far more hostile to new startups than it used to be.” Besides his objections to the way the SEC has increased its oversight of crypto, he is also upset that a stepped-up interest in antitrust has made it more difficult for him to exit investments. “Regulatory agencies are punitively blocking startups from being acquired by the same big companies the government is preferencing in so many other ways,” Andreessen writes. After all, the Federal Trade Commission has launched an inquiry into Big Tech’s partnerships and investments with startups — with the goal of seeing if those partnerships squash competition. The irony is so obvious it’s almost embarrassing to point it out. Andreessen says he is upset that Big Tech is too powerful, but he opposes antitrust action because that blocks a route for VCs to exit. Either you’re comfortable with Big Tech getting bigger, in which case acquisitions are fine, or you want little tech to be competitive, which means blocking industry consolidation. Mainly, it seems that Andreessen believes in cashing out. In the podcast, Andreessen and Horowitz pointedly name Google as a threat to startups. “Google, I think we would all agree, is more powerful than probably 95 percent of countries in the world,” Horowitz says at one point. Google, specifically, is a sore spot with the right wing. Vice presidential nominee Vance has already said it should be broken up. Vance believes Google is controlling information and skewing too far left. Of course, Google’s moderation policies don’t just apply to Google News — they also affect YouTube, which hosts a great many right-wing podcasts without issue. It’s unclear how seriously to take Andreessen and Horowitz’s complaints about Big Tech because the complaints don’t quite square with their behavior. For instance, Facebook is similarly powerful and influential, especially in AI. Andreessen sits on its board. A16z is invested in OpenAI, which has a partnership with Microsoft — and both have lobbied strenuously for more regulation around AI. It sure seems like if a16z wants to change things at those big companies, someone could simply pick up the phone. At this point in the podcast, you could squint and say maybe the concern about AI and crypto is really about technology and progress. But from those two topics, we move on to classic rich guy shit of the most tedious kind: tax reform. Andreessen says it was “the final straw for me. This is the thing that tipped me hard.” They are upset about a proposal to alter capital gains taxes. Capital gains are paid on investment assets, and they are typically paid when the investment is sold and the gains are, in industry terms, “realized.” The new Biden treasury proposal means that for people whose wealth is worth more than $100 million, any unrealized capital gains will be taxed, too. This is what has Andreessen and Horowitz in a tizzy. It means that if they own a clutch of highly valued startup shares, they will have to pay taxes on them before they cash out. This is a “very scary proposal,” Horowitz says. Startups are illiquid assets, Andreessen points out. “Startups never go up and down. They’re never overvalued,” says Horowtiz, dryly. “There’s no bubbles.” Andreessen notes that the way the value of a startup is calculated for the purposes of this proposed tax has to do with the latest round’s valuation. Historically, one of the ways that Andreessen Horowitz has approached startup investing is to inflate a company’s valuation; it is “the OG when it comes to doling out speculative startup valuations.” The new proposed tax punishes this kind of behavior — a high valuation means a high tax. “This makes startups completely implausible,” says Andreessen. “Venture capital just ends. Firms like ours don’t exist.” This is followed by an anxiety spiral that is sort of difficult to convey in text; I suggest you listen for yourself. “California is done,” says Andreessen. “It’s total destruction.” The taxes won’t just target the wealthy; they’ll come for everyone. “Once the structure gets established, the politicians do what they do: they’ll walk the numbers up,” Andreessen says. “Presto chango, we’re Argentina!” says Horowitz. Finally, Horowitz gets ahold of himself. “By the way, this one probably won’t get all the way through the system,” he says. “But it might!” There is another issue that might cause wreckage throughout Silicon Valley. It is immigration. An awful lot of immigrants comprise Silicon Valley’s talent pool — a huge swath of engineers in the US are on H-1B visas. The Trump / Vance ticket is virulently anti-immigrant. The current CEOs of Google, Microsoft, Adobe, and IBM are all immigrants. So are Peter Thiel and Elon Musk. Mark Zuckerberg and Bill Gates are involved in Fwd.us, a lobbying group dedicated to immigration reform that Musk and Sacks both left. If there were an issue that would rally the people who care most about progress, innovation, and talent, you’d think protecting the immigrants who’ve built lives and careers in tech would be it. Stopping immigration is a core issue of the Trump campaign. During the Republican National Convention, delegates held up signs saying “Mass Deportation Now.” Trump has called the H-1B, the visa many tech workers use to come to Silicon Valley, “very bad” and “unfair” to US workers. In his previous term, he targeted H-1B visa applications specifically; in the fiscal year 2018, almost 25 percent of applications were denied, up from about 13 percent the year before. In fiscal year 2019, 20 percent of H-1B applications were denied. The denials plummeted after several Trump administration rules were thrown out by courts; the denial rate in 2022 was just 2 percent. Immigration plainly matters for crypto — as Ethereum founder Vitalik Buterin says, “The crypto industry is uniquely international, and so immigration law is crypto law.” Buterin is one of the most influential voices in crypto, and Ethereum is the foundation for a swath of Andreessen Horowitz’s investment portfolio. Among the investments that rely on it are MakerDAO, VeeFriends, Dapper Labs, and EigenLayer. It is remarkable that the founder of Ethereum is saying that voting for Trump is against the crypto ethos, and the big crypto investors are doing it anyway. The word “immigration” is only mentioned by Andreessen and Horowitz in the podcast when they discuss the rally in which someone attempted an assassination: Trump had turned his head to look at a chart that purported to show illegal immigration into the US as the bullet whizzed by. I wondered why such an important issue for tech wasn’t addressed, so I emailed Margit Wennmachers, a16z’s PR guru, to ask. She didn’t reply. After I finished listening to the podcast, a few things kept nagging at me. Take the very beginning of the podcast. Once upon a time, Andreessen says, you could get very rich and then give the money away in philanthropy, “and you get enormous credit for that. And, you know, it absolves you of whatever.” At some point in the last 10 years, some people suggested that maybe rich people should pay more taxes instead of giving their money away — that perhaps the whims of some random rich person are not the best way to support the most vulnerable in our society. Andreessen and Horowitz suggest that this critique of philanthropy is simply jealousy. It also unbalanced “the deal.” “The deal,” as described on the podcast, is vague. To my ear, it sounds like this: Tech companies could basically do whatever they wanted, as long as people who worked there paid high taxes and donated enough money to charitable causes. The money — taxes, donations — made them the good guys. Andreessen and Horowitz point to the mid-2010s — that is, the era of low interest rates — as the time of “the deal” unraveling. Notably, this is around the time that the tech hype cycle became obvious even to people who weren’t paying attention. This year, it’s scooters! Now it’s viral media companies! Now it’s metaverse! Now it’s crypto! Now it’s AI! These ideas were more or less rejected by the market, except possibly AI. The one thing all these hype cycles had in common was VCs talking their books, as publicly as possible. That charge was led by Andreessen Horowitz. So now, instead of investing in things the market wants, Andreessen and Horowitz appear to be gambling on legislation instead. Their timing is remarkable; not even a week after their Trump endorsement, Biden dropped out of the race, rallying the Democrats behind Vice President Kamala Harris. In the hours immediately following the announcement, small-money donors raised $46.7 million for her campaign. By endorsing Trump, Andreessen and Horowitz have effectively lost whatever leverage they might have had with the Harris campaign. But maybe that doesn’t matter. Near the end of the podcast, Horowitz says that he was shaken by the assassination attempt on Donald Trump because he’s friends with Ivanka, his daughter, and Jared Kushner, his son-in-law. “Ivanka and the kids were just at my house,” Horowitz says, of learning Trump was shot. “We went to see David Copperfield and all that. So my brain was almost frozen because I had this feeling about, ‘Oh my god, Grandpa just got shot.’” As for Andreessen, he has been inveighing against “woke” capital, engaging in Twitter culture wars, and complaining about what he views as the media’s hostility to free speech for a while now. In Andreessen’s 2023 “Techno-Optimist Manifesto,” he lists what he terms “patron saints” of the movement. They include Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, an Italian futurist who was also the co-author of The Fascist Manifesto; Nick Land, whose writing is a foundational text for the so-called alt-right; Neven Sesardic, a philosopher who argues that race is biologically real and not socially constructed; and Vilfredo Pareto, who argued that democracy is an illusion. And this talk about democracy brings me to Curtis Yarvin, personal friend of vice presidential candidate Vance. Yarvin, a software developer, is openly anti-democracy. (Yarvin’s recent newsletter, in response to Biden dropping out, enthusiastically advocates for a return to monarchy. Freak shit.) One of Yarvin’s ideas, called “retire all government employees” or RAGE, is part of Project 2025, a Heritage Foundation proposal for what Trump should do if he wins. This rhetoric was echoed by Vance in 2021, who called out Yarvin by name. So this VC cabal is trading against the basic principles of America — not merely against personal freedom, but democracy itself — in the hopes of profit. It’s not the first time tech has made the trade against freedom; IBM made it during the Holocaust. In venture capital, you are what you fund. Andreessen and Horowitz understand this, even embody it. But they aren’t just funding the issues they discuss on their podcast; they are funding Trump and Vance. That means those donations are anti-abortion, anti-immigration, and possibly even anti-democracy because that is what the Trump / Vance ticket stands for. These are not subsidiary issues: these are now what two of Silicon Valley’s most prominent figures now stand for, too. Is that a good investment? Correction July 24: An earlier version of this article misstated the donation strategy of a crypto super PAC. The group also spends money on Democratic candidates, not just right-wing ones.

articles.title: Knäade Nick Alinia – frias
articles.summary: Vänsteraktivisten Andreas Klominek åtalades för att ha knäat högeraktivisten Nick Alinia i ansiktet. Nu frias han i tingsrätten – som bedömer att han agerade i nödvärn.
articles.body_text: Vänsteraktivisten Andreas Klominek åtalades för att ha knäat högeraktivisten Nick Alinia i ansiktet. Nu frias han i tingsrätten – som bedömer att han agerade i nödvärn. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Det var i maj i år som en närstående till Andreas Klominek hamnade i bråk med högeraktivisten Nick Alinia . Händelseförloppet fångades till viss del på film, som har publicerats i Nick Alinias kanaler och använts bland bevisningen. Bland annat framgår att den yngre mannen, som var delvis maskerad, hetsade mot Alinia och bland annat kallade honom nedsättande ord och slog en mobiltelefon ur hans hand vid två tillfällen, enligt tingsrätten. Under tumultet fick Alinia ner mannen, som är i 18-årsåldern, på marken. Andreas Klominek försökte då få den andra mannen fri och knäade Alinia i huvudet, enligt tingsrättens dom. Tingsrätten kommer i sin dom fram till att Klominek gjort sig skyldig till misshandel, men att det handlat om en putativ nödvärnssituation – att han felaktigt trodde att han befann sig i en nödvärnssituation, även kallad inbillat nödvärn. Andreas Klominek frikänns därför från brott. Den yngre maskerade mannen döms för ofredande mot Alinia, med ett straffvärde på bötesnivå. Klominek dömdes tidigare i år för hot respektive ofredande mot M-ministrarna Benjamin Dousa och Johan Forssell. Detta är en nyhetsartikel. Expressen granskar, avslöjar och ger dig senaste nyheterna på ett sakligt sätt. Mer om oss här. Vill du tipsa oss om något? Skicka in det här!

articles.body_text: Läget i Ukraina är ”mycket allvarligt”, säger bistånds- och utrikeshandelsminister Benjamin Dousa (M). Regeringen lägger därför fram ett vinterpaket till det krigsdrabbade landet, som består av drygt en halv miljard kronor. – Vi jobbar nu intensivt med att även andra länder ska göra allt vad de kan för Ukrainas skull, säger han. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Det nya stödpaketet består av 522 miljoner kronor. Drygt hälften ska gå till energistöd via ett FN-program, med anledning av Rysslands ökade fokus på civil infrastruktur och energiinfrastruktur. – Det har att göra med två saker. Dels att Ryssland ger sig på det nu och dels att vi går in under vinterhalvåret när det kommer bli väldigt, väldigt kallt i Ukraina, säger Benjamin Dousa (M), bistånds- och utrikeshandelsminister i övergångsregeringen. Just energiinfrastrukturen har hamnat i blickfånget den senaste tiden, efter att USA:s president Donald Trump ingått ett dieselavtal med Rysslands Vladimir Putin. Trump har även uppmanat Ukraina till att sluta attackera ryska raffinaderier. Sverige och andra ”vänner till Ukraina” måste nu fortsätta sätta press på den ryska ekonomin, säger Benjamin Dousa. – Det här dieselavtalet gör ju tvärtemot det, det vill säga hjälper Ryssland att kunna exportera mer av en av sina viktigaste råvaror. – Alla steg bortifrån det, där man inte sätter maximal press på den ryska ekonomin, är ju så klart olyckligt, säger ministern. Dousa understryker även vikten av ukrainsk tillgång till satellitsystemet Starlink. Ukrainas tillgång till systemet begränsades tidigare i veckan. Enligt källor till Reuters var det på order från Vita huset. – Varje dag ser vi barn och ungdomar som dödas av aggressiva ryska attacker. Och när man då tappar flera minuter på att inte få tillgång till information om när drönare eller ballistiska robotar lyfter mot Ukraina, så är det verkligen en fråga om liv och död, säger Benjamin Dousa.

articles.title: Efter kryssraketen – vill ändra lagen
articles.summary: Vänsterpartisten Mohamed Ali kryssade sig in i riksdagen efter sju månader som svensk medborgare. Nu vill moderaten Louise Meijer att grundlagen ändras.
articles.body_text: Vänsterpartisten Mohamed Ali kryssade sig in i riksdagen efter sju månader som svensk medborgare. Nu vill moderaten Louise Meijer att grundlagen ändras. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Ali blev svensk medborgare i februari och valdes oväntat in i riksdagen via personkryss i september. Louise Meijer, riksdagsledamot för Moderaterna , vill nu att Sverige inför en kvalifikationstid för att kunna väljas till riksdagen. En person bör ha varit svensk medborgare i tio år, skriver hon. ” En kvalifikationstid ger den enskilde möjlighet att under en längre period leva som svensk medborgare, delta i samhället och fördjupa sin förståelse för de institutioner och demokratiska principer som en riksdagsledamot ska företräda ”, skriver hon i en enskild motion. Sådana krav finns i andra länder, fortsätter hon och nämner sju års medborgarskap i USA för att väljas till representanthuset och sex år i Argentina för val till senaten. articles.summary: Jan Emanuel säljer ett helt kvarter i Norrtälje. Han hoppas få in 50 miljoner kronor och siktar på att köpa nåt dyrare.
articles.body_text: Brist på fastigheter har inte Jan Emanuel. – 50 miljoner någonting räknar jag med att få, säger han. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. För tio år sedan köpte den före detta S-riksdagsledamoten Jan Emanuel ett helt kvarter i centrala Norrtälje. – Det ligger i gamla stan i Norrtälje, jag rustade upp det och gjorde det fint. Och nu ska jag sälja det. Kvarteret består av fyra fastigheter, och omfattar bostadslägenheter och butikslokaler. I objektsbeskrivningen hos mäklaren sägs det att en av fastigheterna ha anor från 1700-talet. – Jag köpte kvarteret för att jag tyckte att det var otroligt vackert. Det är som en saga att gå in i det. – Jag tänkte köpa något dyrare. Och för ett tag sedan insåg jag att det fortfarande är jättevackert, men jag går aldrig där. Jag är på massa andra ställen. Och då är det bättre att låta någon annan som brinner för Norrtälje ta vid och kanske exploaterar det. Men framför allt vill jag att någon som bor och är i Norrtälje tar över. Priset i objektsbeskrivningen är satt till 46 miljoner kronor, men Jan Emanuel tror på mer. – Mäklaren har lagt priset lite under vad det är värt för att storhajarna ska börja buda, om jag har förstått saken rätt. 50 miljoner någonstans räknar jag med. Någon brist på fastigheter har Jan Emanuel inte även om han säljer kvarteret i Norrtälje. – Jag har boende i Palma, på Gran Canaria, Kuba, Gotland, i Stockholm, Uppsala. Säkert något mer ställe, men det är de jag kommer på nu.

articles.title: Palestinska Warda, 66: ”Bosättare slog mig med påkar”
articles.summary: Palestinska Warda, 66: ”Bosättare slog mig med påkar”
articles.body_text: Warda Adili, 66, föll till marken när extrema israeliska bosättare attackerade hennes familj som plockade sina oliver. – De slog mig med påkar, säger den palestinska kvinnan ­– som har bruten handled och armen i band efter misshandeln – i byn Osarin på Västbanken. Våldet mot palestinier ökar varje år när olivskörden börjar. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Den ockuperade Västbanken är en krutdurk som kan explodera när som helst. Årets olivskörd har just inletts och liksom varje år trappar bosättare då upp våldet mot palestinier. Två människor har dödats, tiotals har skadats och över 100 incidenter har rapporterats de tio första dagarna, enligt israeliska människorättsorganisationer. Israeliska bosättares våld mot palestinier ökar under olivskörden – och spänningen stiger på Västbanken. Två palestinier har dödats och tiotals skadats under skördens tio första dagar. ”De slog mig med påkar”, säger Warda Adili, 66, i byn Osarin som attackerades när hon och familjen plockade oliver. – Vi var ute och plockade oliver, hela familjen. Då kom de plötsligt. Först kastade de sten, när de kom närmare slog de mig med påkar, säger Warda Adili i sitt hem i byn Osarin på Västbanken – där familjens olivodling ligger på andra sidan gatan. – Jag föll till marken. Jag har ont över hela kroppen, jag kan inte äta. Och jag är rädd hela tiden, säger hon. Hon har armen i en svart mitella och ett vitt bandage runt sin brutna handled – och får stöd av familjemedlemmar när hon ska gå över gatan för att visa olivlunden för Expressen och andra medier på plats.
